title: Mind and will (ST I.82)
hookLine: the mind knows the good and the will loves it
tomorrow: Not money, fame, pleasure or power

cards: Which is harder: knowing what's good, or wanting it? A recipe card can tell you exactly how to make soup for a sick friend. It can't get you off the couch to chop the onions.
A friend can explain, clearly and correctly, why you should call your brother. You can agree with every word and still not dial. Between seeing a good and going after it, there's a gap.
Thomas Aquinas names the two powers on either side of it. One sees. One reaches.

teach.b: Thomas calls them the intellect and the will. The intellect knows: it grasps what things are, and sees what's good.
The will is the soul's power to love and choose: it reaches for the good the mind shows it. Then the will sets the mind to work again: find me the way there. Thomas makes a striking claim.

teach.h: IT MUST WANT HAPPINESS, YET IT CHOOSES.
teach.b: The will can't help wanting happiness; that's built in, the way the eye can't help taking in light.
But it isn't forced to choose any particular good on the way, this job or that one, this friend or that habit, because none of them is the whole of happiness. That's where freedom lives.
Then the question everyone wants settled: which is greater? Thomas answers in two parts. In itself, the intellect is the higher power.
But it depends on what it's aimed at.
For things beneath us, knowing them is better than loving them. For God, who is above us, loving God is better than knowing about God. A person can know a great deal of theology and love very little.

teach.h: KNOWLEDGE PUFFETH UP; BUT CHARITY EDIFIETH.
teach.b: Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "Knowledge puffeth up; but charity edifieth." That doesn't make knowing useless. The will can only love what the mind has shown it.
Jesus says, in John: "And you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free." On Thomas's account: know first, but don't stop at knowing.

how: Catholic moral teaching, drawing on Thomas, speaks of the intellect and the will as the two spiritual powers of the soul, and examinations of conscience often ask both what a person knew and what they chose.

o: the brain and the nerves working together
the power that sees and the power that chooses
reason and feelings, always at odds

games.q: mind and will — tap the pairs.
p: the will can't help wanting it

s: for Thomas, the will can choose not to want happiness at all
he says the will can't help wanting happiness. it's free in choosing the particular goods along the way.
Thomas says loving God is better than knowing about God
in itself the intellect is higher, but toward God, who is above us, love outranks knowledge.
for Thomas, mind and will work separately and never affect each other
the mind shows the will a good; the will then sets the mind to work finding the way.

games.q: you're Thomas. a student asks: which is greater, the mind or the will? what do you answer?
o: the mind, always and in every case.
the mind in itself, but toward God, loving is better than knowing.
the will, always and in every case.
games.why: Thomas gives a two-part answer: in itself the intellect is higher, but for things above us, like God, love outranks knowledge.

practice: Bring up one good thing you already know you ought to do and haven't: a thank-you note, a bill, a visit, an apology.

See clearly why it's good, then hand it to the will: picture yourself doing it, step by step, and where you balk, don't argue, just choose it again, quietly. If you pray, ask God for the strength to carry it out.

wordCard.voice: Mind and will. The intellect sees the good; the will loves and chooses it. For Thomas, they work as a pair, and toward God, loving outranks knowing. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: the intellect and the will.

carryVoice: Your line: know, then love. The mind lights the good; the will goes after it. Until tomorrow.
